claim: Gene expression is affected by interactions between local genetic variation and DNA accessibility.
source: Gene expression is known to be affected by interactions between local genetic variation and DNA accessibility, with the latter organized into three-dimensional chromatin structures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact, representing established scientific understanding.

claim: DNA accessibility is organized into three-dimensional chromatin structures.
source: Gene expression is known to be affected by interactions between local genetic variation and DNA accessibility, with the latter organized into three-dimensional chromatin structures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about chromatin organization.

claim: Analyses of genetic-epigenetic interactions have previously been limited.
source: Analyses of these interactions have previously been limited, obscuring their regulatory context, and the extent to which they occur throughout the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of prior research limitations.

claim: The study used embryonic stem cells derived from Diversity Outbred mice.
source: We establish the extent and structure of genotype-by-epigenotype interaction using embryonic stem cells derived from Diversity Outbred mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental system used.

claim: The Diversity Outbred mouse population segregates millions of variants from eight inbred founders.
source: This mouse population segregates millions of variants from eight inbred founders, enabling precision genetic mapping with extensive genotypic and phenotypic diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of the DO mouse population.

claim: 176 samples were profiled for genotype, gene expression, and open chromatin.
source: With 176 samples profiled for genotype, gene expression, and open chromatin, we used regression modeling to infer genetic–epigenetic interactions on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the dataset size and types.

claim: Statistical interactions between genetic variants and chromatin accessibility are common throughout the genome.
source: Our results demonstrate that statistical interactions between genetic variants and chromatin accessibility are common throughout the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding from the regression modeling analysis.

claim: Genetic-epigenetic interactions occur within the local area of the affected gene.
source: We found that these interactions occur within the local area of the affected gene, and that this locality corresponds to topologically associated domains (TADs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the spatial organization of interactions.

claim: The locality of genetic-epigenetic interactions corresponds to topologically associated domains (TADs).
source: We found that these interactions occur within the local area of the affected gene, and that this locality corresponds to topologically associated domains (TADs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding linking interaction locality to TAD structure.

claim: The likelihood of interaction was most strongly defined by three-dimensional domain structure rather than linear DNA sequence.
source: The likelihood of interaction was most strongly defined by the three-dimensional (3D) domain structure rather than linear DNA sequence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the determinants of interaction likelihood.

claim: Stable 3D genome structure is an effective tool to guide searches for regulatory elements.
source: We show that stable 3D genome structure is an effective tool to guide searches for regulatory elements and, conversely, that regulatory elements in genetically diverse populations provide a means to infer 3D genome structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion about the utility of 3D genome structure.

claim: Regulatory elements in genetically diverse populations provide a means to infer 3D genome structure.
source: We show that stable 3D genome structure is an effective tool to guide searches for regulatory elements and, conversely, that regulatory elements in genetically diverse populations provide a means to infer 3D genome structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion about inferring genome structure from regulatory elements.

claim: CTCF ChIP-seq revealed strain-specific binding in the inbred founder mice.
source: We confirmed this finding with CTCF ChIP-seq that revealed strain-specific binding in the inbred founder mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from CTCF ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: Open chromatin participating in the most significant regression models demonstrated an enrichment for developmental genes.
source: In stem cells, open chromatin participating in the most significant regression models demonstrated an enrichment for developmental genes and the TAD-forming CTCF-binding complex, providing an opportunity for statistical inference of shifting TAD boundaries operating during early development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the functional enrichment of interacting open chromatin regions.

claim: Open chromatin participating in the most significant regression models demonstrated an enrichment for the TAD-forming CTCF-binding complex.
source: In stem cells, open chromatin participating in the most significant regression models demonstrated an enrichment for developmental genes and the TAD-forming CTCF-binding complex, providing an opportunity for statistical inference of shifting TAD boundaries operating during early development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding about the enrichment of CTCF-binding sites.

claim: Genetic and epigenetic factors operate within the context of 3D chromatin structure.
source: These findings provide evidence that genetic and epigenetic factors operate within the context of 3D chromatin structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Studies of genetic-epigenetic interactions are generally limited to examination of individual regions or overlapping SNPs and open chromatin peaks.
source: Studies are generally limited to examination of individual regions or overlapping single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and open chromatin peaks with limited investigation into how these regulatory elements combine to affect gene transcription (Ackermann et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Many studies have used a 100- to 500-kb flanking window around a gene to encapsulate the landscape of local epigenetic effects.
source: Many have used a 100- to 500-kb flanking window around a gene to encapsulate the landscape of local epigenetic effects (Veyrieras et al., 2008; Stranger et al., 2007; Dixon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The estimated scale of the local area is approximately equivalent to the size of a topologically associated domain (TAD).
source: Incidentally, the estimated scale of this local area is approximately equivalent to the size of a topologically associated domain (TAD).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about the correspondence between local area definitions and TAD size.

claim: TADs are chromatin loops with an average length of approximately 1.1 Mb.
source: TADs are chromatin loops with an average length of approximately 1.1 Mb that are joined via the architectural protein CTCF and the cohesin protein complex at known binding motifs (Dixon et al., 2012; Pombo and Dillon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TADs are joined via the architectural protein CTCF and the cohesin protein complex at known binding motifs.
source: TADs are chromatin loops with an average length of approximately 1.1 Mb that are joined via the architectural protein CTCF and the cohesin protein complex at known binding motifs (Dixon et al., 2012; Pombo and Dillon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TADs are believed to be mostly cell-type invariant and conserved across species.
source: TADs are believed to be mostly cell-type invariant and conserved across species (Dixon et al., 2012; Harmston et al., 2017; Yakushiji-Kaminatsui et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TADs provide physical boundaries for local regulatory function.
source: The current hypothesis is that TADs provide physical boundaries for local regulatory function, but functional analysis of regulatory interactions within TADs has been limited by the lack of informative genetic variation in the studies that led to TAD discovery.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a current hypothesis in the field.

claim: The Diversity Outbred (DO) mouse population is a heterogeneous stock composed of mice derived from eight founder strains, including three wild-derived strains.
source: The Diversity Outbred (DO) mouse population is a heterogeneous stock composed of mice derived from eight founder strains, including three wild-derived strains (Churchill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ongoing process of random outbreeding in DO mice produces a mouse population segregating millions of precisely mapped SNPs.
source: The ongoing process of random outbreeding produces a mouse population segregating millions of precisely mapped SNPs, with well-balanced allele frequencies, and increasingly small blocks of linkage disequilibrium that now approach the size of TADs (Broman, 2012; Chesler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Blocks of linkage disequilibrium in DO mice now approach the size of TADs.
source: The ongoing process of random outbreeding produces a mouse population segregating millions of precisely mapped SNPs, with well-balanced allele frequencies, and increasingly small blocks of linkage disequilibrium that now approach the size of TADs (Broman, 2012; Chesler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A recent study used mESCs derived from generation 19 DO embryos to study gene regulatory networks that stabilize pluripotent states in vitro.
source: A recent study used mESCs derived from generation 19 DO embryos, grown in the absence of ERK inhibition to study the gene regulatory networks that stabilize pluripotent states in vitro. This revealed phenotypic variability in features of ground state pluripotency (Skelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: 27,509 significant models were identified from 39,021,625 tested combinations.
source: This resulted in 27,509 significant models (Bonferroni adjusted p < 1 × 10−7), or 0.07% of all models, involving 19,145 ATAC-seq peaks, 14,476 variants, and 1286 genes (18.75%, 21.16%, and 8.52% of the total input, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the regression modeling analysis.

claim: The number of significant models was four orders of magnitude greater than expected under a null distribution.
source: If interactions were detected randomly, we would expect a null distribution with no enrichment of low p-value models. Instead, the number of significant models was four orders of magnitude greater than expected, thus indicating the presence of true associations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A showing the p-value distribution.

claim: Approximately half (49%) of all significant interacting models included a genetic variant or ATAC peak within 4 Mb of the gene they affected.
source: Approximately half (49%) of all significant interacting models included a genetic variant or ATAC peak within 4 Mb of the gene they affected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the spatial distribution of interactions.

claim: Less than 10% of variants and ATAC peaks clustered closer to each other than they did to the gene they affected.
source: Within this range, we found that less than 10% of variants and ATAC peaks clustered closer to each other than they did to the gene they affected, indicating that co-localization may not the driving factor in many interacting models (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the spatial relationships of interacting elements.

claim: Models with at least one interacting element within the same TAD as the gene were 3.7 times more likely to reach the significance threshold compared to models that did not.
source: Models with at least one interacting element within the same TAD as the gene were 3.7 times more likely to reach our threshold, compared to models that did not (3.3% vs. 0.9%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the enrichment of intra-TAD interactions.

claim: Interacting models represented 32.29% of significant intra-TAD models.
source: To this end, we compared interacting models, found to represent 32.29% of significant intra-TAD models (Figure 2C), with models associated with genetic variants or ATAC-seq peaks without interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: 26.35% of genetic variants are shared between non-additive interacting models and additive models.
source: We found that 26.35% of genetic variants are shared between non-additive interacting models and additive models, and 23.12% are shared with models that contain no ATAC-seq peak contribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the overlap of genetic variants across model types.

claim: 41.81% of ATAC-seq peaks are exclusive to interacting models.
source: In contrast, few models contain only an ATAC-seq peak contribution, and 41.81% of ATAC-seq peaks are exclusive to interacting models (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: 52,511 ATAC-seq peaks share a TAD with their interacting gene, versus 24,229 peaks in different TADs or inter-TAD regions.
source: With a window of 200 kb on either side of an active CTCF boundary, we found 52,511 ATAC-seq peaks sharing a TAD with their interacting gene, versus 24,229 peaks in different TADs or inter-TAD regions
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the distribution of ATAC-seq peaks relative to TAD boundaries.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of intra-TAD gene–peak interactions over expectations based on overall ATAC-seq peak density (odds ratio of 1.48, null expectation p < 2.2 × 10−16).
source: This constitutes a significant enrichment of intra-TAD gene–peak interactions over expectations based on overall ATAC-seq peak density (an odds ratio of 1.48, null expectation p < 2.2 × 10−16) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: 29 individual ATAC-seq peaks were involved in more than 200 non-additive interactions each.
source: We also identified 29 individual ATAC-seq peaks that were involved in more than 200 non-additive interactions each, which are distinctly visible within the aggregate view (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure.

claim: To capture 95% of inter-TAD genetic–epigenetic interactions at adjusted p < 1 × 10−7, a window of 2,074,778 bp upstream and 2,575,581 bp downstream of the gene TSS was required.
source: We found that to capture 95% of inter-TAD genetic–epigenetic interactions at adjusted p < 1 × 10−7, a window of 2,074,778 bp upstream and 2,575,581 bp downstream of the gene TSS was required (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: 65.37% of ATAC-seq peaks on each chromosome fell within gene bodies.
source: 65.37% of peaks on each chromosome fell within gene bodies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the genomic distribution of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 34.41% of ATAC-seq peaks fall within exons, half of which fell within the first (or only) exon.
source: Normalized for length, exons were especially enriched, with 34.41% of peaks falling within exons, half of which fell within the first (or only) exon.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the distribution of ATAC-seq peaks in exons.

claim: 24.06% of ATAC-seq peaks overlap with promoters.
source: 24.06% of peaks overlap with promoters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the overlap of ATAC-seq peaks with promoters.

claim: 6.09% of ATAC-seq peaks fall within enhancers curated for ESC R, R1, KH2 embryonic stem cell lines.
source: 6.09% of peaks fall within enhancers curated for ESC R, R1, KH2 embryonic stem cell lines.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the overlap of ATAC-seq peaks with enhancers.

claim: The gene-centric increase in regulatory interaction density responds to the 3D context of the TAD loop, crossing CTCF boundaries irrespective of linear DNA sequence.
source: This revealed that the gene-centric increase in regulatory interaction density responded to the 3D context of the TAD loop, crossing CTCF boundaries irrespective of linear DNA sequence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the spatial organization of interactions.

claim: TAD-based searches produce consistently higher percentages of interacting ATAC-seq peaks across the analysis compared to linear sequence-based searches.
source: We found that TAD-based searches produce consistently higher percentages of interacting ATAC-seq peaks across the analysis, and higher ATAC-seq peak density out to ±~1 Mb.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between search methods.

claim: 24.31% of genes (12,437 genes) were found to have a TAD boundary close upstream to their TSS.
source: We found that while the majority of genes were randomly distributed within their TADs, 12,437 or 24,2124.31% of genes were found to have a TAD boundary close upstream to their TSS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure.

claim: Interaction effects were of greater absolute value than ATAC-seq effects 61.24% of the time.
source: However, in the context of non-additive genetic–epigenetic interactions we observed interaction effects of greater absolute value than ATAC-seq effects 61.24% of the time, greater than genotypic variant coefficients 11.42% of the time, and greater than both main effects 8.52% of the time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the relative magnitudes of regression coefficients.

claim: Models indicating redundancy or interference were the most common overall, totaling 40.53–39.54% of all models.
source: We found that models indicating redundancy or interference were the most common overall, totaling 40.53–39.54% of all models (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the distribution of model types.

claim: Synergistic effects were found in 17.02% of all models.
source: Synergistic effects were found in 17.02% of all models.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the frequency of synergistic effects.

claim: An increase in ATAC-seq signal had a negative effect on gene expression in 40.76% of models.
source: While ATAC-seq peaks are often correlated with increased gene expression (Cao et al., 2018), we were surprised to find that an increase in ATAC-seq signal had a negative effect on gene expression in 40.76% of models (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the directionality of ATAC-seq effects.

claim: The negative effector subset was enriched for 49 motifs, including the CTCF-binding site (p < 2.0 × 10−14) and SMAD3-binding site (p < 1.5 × 10−8).
source: Results showed the negative effector subset was enriched for 49 motifs (Supplementary file 7), including the CTCF-binding site (p < 2.0 × 10−14) and SMAD3-binding site (p < 1.5 × 10−8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from motif enrichment analysis.

claim: 53.3% of top negative ATAC-seq sequences had at least one CTCF-binding motif in them, compared to 35.3% in ATAC-seq peaks with positive effectors on gene transcription.
source: FIMO motif scanning showed that 53.3% of top negative ATAC-seq sequences had at least one CTCF-binding motif in them, compared to 35.3% in ATAC-seq peaks with positive effectors on gene transcription (see deposited data).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from FIMO motif scanning.

claim: 96.1% of CTCF motifs within the negative subset were found to contain SNPs from the non-reference DO founder strains, versus 18.0% for positive effect-associated CTCF motifs (p < 2.2 × 10−16).
source: Out of CTCF motifs within this negative subset, 96.1% of these were found to contain SNPs from the non-reference DO founder strains, versus 18.0% for positive effect-associated CTCF motifs (p < 2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about SNP distribution in CTCF motifs.

claim: 2.04% and 1.87% of ENCODE CTCF ChIP-seq peaks overlapped with negative ATAC effect CTCF-binding sites that contained SNPs, versus 17.45% and 16.20% overlapping with positive effect CTCF-binding sites that contained SNPs.
source: Comparing to available ENCODE CTCF ChIP-seq in C57BL/6 Bruce4 and 129/Ola E14TG2a.4 mESCs (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Shen et al., 2012), we found 2.04% and 1.87% of these overlapped with negative ATAC effect CTCF-binding sites that contained SNPs, versus 17.45% and 16.20% overlapping with positive effect CTCF-binding sites that contained SNPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from comparison with ENCODE data.

claim: Platr2's TAD contains 1031 models of non-additive genotype–ATAC interaction reaching the significance cutoff for resident genes, of which 179 were models of Platr2 expression.
source: Platr2's TAD contains a high concentration of confidently called regression models in our analysis (Supplementary file 8), with 1031 models of non-additive genotype–ATAC interaction reaching our significance cutoff for resident genes, of which 179 were models of Platr2 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about Platr2's regulatory landscape.

claim: Previous studies have found a group of genes regulated in trans by expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) mapped to Platr2.
source: Previous studies have found a group of genes regulated in trans by expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) mapped to Platr2 (Skelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Motif enrichment analysis of interacting ATAC-seq peaks in Platr2's TAD identified a sequence at 16 sites which contain Smad3-binding motifs, and another sequence at 15 sites that contain CTCF-binding motifs.
source: Motif enrichment analysis of interacting ATAC-seq peaks identified a sequence at 16 sites which contain Smad3-binding motifs, and another sequence at 15 sites that contain CTCF-binding motifs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B, Supplementary file 9), which may suggest modulation of CTCF-binding strength.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: CTCF ChIP-seq was performed on mESCs derived from four of the eight DO founder strains.
source: To test this, we performed CTCF ChIP-seq on mESCs derived from four of the eight DO founder strains, including representatives from the three subspecies contributing to the DO population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental design.

claim: Sample ChIP-seq-binding intensities clustered by strain with principal component analysis (PCA), and were separated by subspecies as expected.
source: Sample ChIP-seq-binding intensities clustered by strain with principal component analysis (PCA), and were separated by subspecies as expected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure.

claim: 65,541 ChIP-seq peaks passed the significance threshold (found in at least two samples in at least one strain), or 68.21% of results.
source: Across all samples, 65,541 ChIP-seq peaks passed our significance threshold (found in at least two samples in at least one strain), or 68.21% of results.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: 90.65% of significant ChIP-seq peaks overlapped with the publicly available TAD dataset.
source: 90.65% of these overlapped with the publicly available TAD dataset we had employed for our previous analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the overlap between ChIP-seq peaks and TADs.

claim: 52% of CTCF ChIP-seq peaks were shared across all four strains, with the remaining 48% found in three or fewer strains.
source: Fifty-two percent of CTCF ChIP-seq peaks were shared across all four strains, with the remaining 48% found in three or fewer strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: 23,887 significant CTCF ChIP-seq peaks overlapped with CTCF-binding sites that had been previously identified, or 36.45% overlap with significant results.
source: We found 23,887 of our significant CTCF ChIP-seq peaks these overlapped with CTCF-binding sites that had been previously identified, or 36.45% overlap with significant results.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the overlap with previously identified sites.

claim: 13% of CTCF ChIP-seq peaks had a variance in fold enrichment greater than 10.
source: Our analysis found a range of binding intensities at individual loci, with 13% having a variance in fold enrichment greater than 10 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The proportion of results below p < 0.05 in all CTCF ChIP-seq peaks was 16%.
source: The proportion of results below p < 0.05 in all CTCF ChIP-seq peaks was 16%, establishing a baseline of predictive power for SNPs genome-wide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a baseline finding.

claim: Subsetting to CTCF-binding sites found in ATAC-seq peaks increased the proportion of significant correlation to 31%.
source: Subsetting to those CTCF-binding sites found in ATAC-seq peaks increased the proportion of significant correlation to 31%.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the predictive power of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Binding sites associated with non-additive interacting models had 37% correlation with CTCF-binding intensity.
source: Binding sites associated with non-additive interacting models had 37% correlation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the predictive power of interacting models.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks that were negative effectors in interacting regression models produced a 39% correlation with CTCF-binding intensity.
source: Subsetting those ATAC-seq peaks that were negative effectors in interacting regression models produced a 39% correlation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about the predictive power of negative effector peaks.

claim: In regions associated with a greater than average number of regression models, the gap between negative and positive effector regions widened to 44% versus 27% correlation.
source: Results showed that the gap between negative and positive effector regions widened in these regions to 44% versus 27% correlation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding about regions with high model density.

claim: Integrating analysis of multi-omics data in a genetically diverse population allows for greater specificity and modeling of complex regulatory interactions.
source: Integrating analysis of multi-omics data in a genetically diverse population allows for greater specificity and modeling of complex regulatory interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion about the approach.

claim: Patterns of genetic–epigenetic interaction reflect the structure of topologically associating domains.
source: From our analysis of genetic–epigenetic interactions we have put forth several key findings regarding the interactivity, structure, and function in the regulation of gene expression. We discovered that patterns of genetic–epigenetic interaction reflect the structure of topologically associating domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding.

claim: Open chromatin density is less important for interactivity than TAD boundaries are.
source: While open chromatin density is higher within TADs, we found that open chromatin density is less important for interactivity than TAD boundaries are.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Linear proximity cannot be used to identify association between genes and regulatory features.
source: Furthermore, linear proximity cannot be used to identify association between genes and regulatory features.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion about the limitations of linear distance measures.

claim: Almost half of CTCF binding is strain specific in mESCs.
source: Our results indicated that almost half of CTCF binding is strain specific in mESCs, with imputed links to genetic variants in the DO mouse population.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: Small changes in TAD boundary location are previously indicated to be involved in developmental and differentiation processes.
source: Small changes in TAD boundary location are previously indicated to be involved in developmental and differentiation processes (Rodríguez-Carballo et al., 2020; Andrey et al., 2013; Takayama et al., 2021), and other studies have shown that chromatin rearrangement that alters TAD boundaries is linked to cancer development (Dixon et al., 2012; Tyler et al., 2016; Menghi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Chromatin rearrangement that alters TAD boundaries is linked to cancer development.
source: Small changes in TAD boundary location are previously indicated to be involved in developmental and differentiation processes (Rodríguez-Carballo et al., 2020; Andrey et al., 2013; Takayama et al., 2021), and other studies have shown that chromatin rearrangement that alters TAD boundaries is linked to cancer development (Dixon et al., 2012; Tyler et al., 2016; Menghi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Including TAD boundaries and TAD loops in analyzing genomic features affecting gene expression can maximize and contextualize results.
source: These findings imply that including TAD boundaries and TAD loops in analyzing genomic features affecting gene expression, such as chromatin states and genetic variants, can maximize and contextualize results.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion about analytical approaches.

claim: DO mESC production was performed by Predictive Biology.
source: DO mESC production was performed by Predictive Biology.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a description of sample production.

claim: Cultures were grown with G3SK inhibitor (1i medium).
source: Cultures were grown with G3SK inhibitor (1i medium).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a description of culture conditions.

claim: RNA-seq resulted in 6M-55M 2 × 75 bp paired-end (PE) reads per sample.
source: RNA-seq resulted in 6M-55M 2 × 75 bp paired-end (PE) reads per sample.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a description of sequencing depth.

claim: Expression data were formatted and analyzed as log2-transformed transcripts per million (TPM).
source: Expression data were formatted and analyzed as log2-transformed transcripts per million (TPM).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a description of data processing.

claim: ATAC-seq data were formatted as trimmed mean of M values (TMM).
source: ATAC-seq data were formatted as trimmed mean of M values (TMM) (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Genotyping was performed by Giga Mouse Universal Genotyping Array (GigaMUGA), an Illumina Infinium array of 143,000 SNP markers.
source: Genotyping was performed by Giga Mouse Universal Genotyping Array (GigaMUGA), an Illumina Infinium array of 143,000 SNP markers with a special focus on DO founder strains (Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Sample genotypes were estimated using a previously calculated grid of 68,413 GigaMUGA pseudoprobes evenly spaced by genetic distance.
source: Sample genotypes were estimated in reflection of linkage disequilibrium and haplotype prediction confidence, employing a previously calculated grid of GigaMUGA pseudoprobes, which were evenly spaced by genetic distance (Bubier et al., 2020, Chick et al., 2016). This produced a subset of 68,413 imputed haplotype calls centered at specific loci which were most likely to match the actual haplotype in each region (Supplementary Information).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.

claim: A Bonferroni adjusted p value cutoff of p < 1 × 10−7 was selected for significant models.
source: Given the possibility of overfitting as the number of model terms increases and the high number of models tested (see Results), a Bonferroni adjusted p value cutoff of p < 1 × 10−7 was selected (hereafter referred to as 'significant models').
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a description of the significance threshold.

claim: mESC TAD data were derived from previously published work by Dixon et al., 2012.
source: mESC TAD data were derived from previously published work (Dixon et al., 2012). in a liftover from mm9 to mm10 via UCSC genome browser (Kuhn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.

claim: DNA motif and binding site discovery were performed using the MEMEsuite tools MEME, STREME, and Tomtom.
source: DNA motif and binding site discovery were performed using the MEMEsuite tools MEME, STREME, and Tomtom, all set to default parameters (see Supplemental Data) (Bailey et al., 2009; Bailey and Elkan, 1994; Bailey, 2020; Gupta et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.

claim: CTCF ChIP-seq was performed following previously established protocols.
source: We performed CTCF ChIP-seq following previously established protocols (Oomen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Three cell lines were run for four isogenic mESC strains: C57BL/6J, CAST/EiJ, PWK/Ph, and WSB/EiJ.
source: Three cell lines were run for four isogenic mESC strains, C57BL/6J, CAST/EiJ, PWK/Ph, and WSB/EiJ.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a description of the ChIP-seq experimental design.
